title: Locating Irrationals on the Number Line

steps.body: Once √n sits between two whole numbers, narrow further with decimals — testing 7.0², 7.1², 7.2²… — the same squeezing idea, one decimal place at a time.
The line has no gaps — irrationals live in them.

widget.prompt: Place π to two decimal places.
widget.successFeedback: 3.14 — but only to two places. π keeps going forever without repeating, and it still has ONE exact spot on this line. Every point on the line is a real number, and most of them cannot be written as fractions at all.
widget.lowFeedback: Below π. It sits just past 3.1.
widget.highFeedback: Above π. It stops short of 3.15.

predict.prompt: Before you place it: is 3.14 closer to 3 or to 4?
predict.reveal: 3.14 sits 0.14 from 3 and 0.86 from 4 — the 3 side wins. Judging position from the endpoints first makes the exact placement easier to defend.

steps.body: The same idea applies to π: since π ≈ 3.14159…, at one decimal place π ≈ 3.1. We could keep narrowing to as many decimal places as we want — the digits just never stop or repeat.

explanationVariants: √10 ≈ 3.162, which rounds up to 3.2 at one decimal place.
3.1² = 9.61 undershoots 10, and 3.2² = 10.24 overshoots it, so √10 rounds to 3.2.

commonErrors.feedback: √10 ≈ 3.162, which rounds UP to 3.2, not down to 3.1.
That's just the whole-number bound, not the one-decimal estimate — try 3.2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √10 ≈ 3.162, so to one decimal place it's 3.2.

commonErrors.feedback: √2 ≈ 1.414, which rounds DOWN to 1.4, not up to 1.5.
That's just the whole-number bound — try 1.4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √2 ≈ 1.414, so to one decimal place it's 1.4.

explanationVariants: √3 ≈ 1.732, which rounds down to 1.7 at one decimal place.
1.7² = 2.89 undershoots 3, and 1.8² = 3.24 overshoots it, so √3 rounds to 1.7.

commonErrors.feedback: √3 ≈ 1.732, which rounds DOWN to 1.7, not up to 1.8.
That's not even the right whole-number bound — 1² = 1 and 2² = 4 trap √3 between 1 and 2, closer to 1.7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √3 ≈ 1.732, so to one decimal place it's 1.7.

5.1² = 26.01 undershoots 27, and 5.2² = 27.04 overshoots it, so √27 rounds to 5.2.

commonErrors.feedback: √27 ≈ 5.196, which rounds UP to 5.2, not down to 5.1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √27 ≈ 5.196, so to one decimal place it's 5.2.

explanationVariants: √83 ≈ 9.110, which rounds to 9.1 at one decimal place.
9.1² = 82.81 undershoots 83, and 9.2² = 84.64 overshoots it, so √83 rounds to 9.1.

commonErrors.feedback: √83 ≈ 9.11, which rounds DOWN to 9.1, not up to 9.2.
That's just the whole-number bound — narrow further to one decimal place: 9.1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √83 ≈ 9.110, so to one decimal place it's 9.1.

hints: First bracket √83 between whole numbers: 9² = 81 and 10² = 100, so it's between 9 and 10.
Now test tenths: 9.1² = 82.81 and 9.2² = 84.64 — where does 83 fall?
82.81 < 83 < 84.64, so √83 rounds to 9.1 at one decimal place.

steps.body: Narrow with decimals the same way as with whole numbers.
takeaways: Test tenths (7.0², 7.1², 7.2², …) to narrow a bracket to one decimal place.
Every irrational number can be approximated to any precision this way.
The approximation never becomes exact — the true value never terminates or repeats.
steps.teaser: Next: comparing and estimating expressions that mix rationals and irrationals.

concept.body: To narrow √n to one decimal place, test tenths near its whole-number bracket (e.g. 7.0², 7.1², 7.2²) and see which two straddle n.

explanationVariants: √5 ≈ 2.236, which rounds to 2.2 at one decimal place.
2.2² = 4.84 undershoots 5, and 2.3² = 5.29 overshoots it, so √5 rounds to 2.2.
